topic.timeline_arc: Mid‑2025 saw India’s IPO market reignited by regulatory settlements and cross‑border financing, sparking a wave of large offerings. By late summer, tech‑sector volatility tempered enthusiasm, yet corporate leaders and AI investors kept the pipeline active, leading to record oversubscriptions and a festival‑season boom in September. October highlighted a shift in global finance hubs and the looming trillion‑dollar OpenAI IPO, while November‑December expanded the scope to multinational listings and post‑IPO challenges in Asian tech firms. Entering 2026, mega IPOs persisted amid market volatility and rising political‑legal turbulence, suggesting that future offerings will be shaped by both investor appetite and external uncertainties.
turning_points: Regulatory settlements (SEBI observations, NSE settlement) cleared hurdles and revived IPO activity in India.
Record oversubscription of Urban Company and festival‑season surge demonstrated intense investor demand and broadened the IPO pipeline.
OpenAI’s trillion‑dollar IPO prospect and London dropping out of the top‑20 IPO hubs signaled a global re‑allocation of listing destinations.

text.summary: Coverage of the IPO market runs to 184,831 articles between 2024-06 and 2026-05, and its direction is rising, with the last third of the window at 1.35 times the first third. Output peaked in 2025-09 at 12,966 articles. The tone is markedly more positive than ordinary news coverage, with 0.23 negative articles per positive one against 0.58 for all news. Coverage is driven by Indian listings, regulatory settlements, large offerings and the prospect of AI-linked mega IPOs. Of the stories, 120,525 fall in the top priority bands, which does not measure tone.

text.aud1: On the claim that IPOs are underpriced on the first trading day, the wider corpus of 32,707 papers has 14,089 supporting, 6,126 qualifying, 1,262 contradicting and 11,230 neutral, with 22.6 percent contested. The selected documents read give a weaker picture: 1 supports, 0 contradict, 0 qualify, 9 are unrelated and 0 are unread, and the recommendation is that this sample does not establish scientific consensus. In the head-to-head, the first claim is judged to have more evidence behind it than the claim that IPOs underperform the market in the long run, which has 112 papers touching both poles and 33.0 percent contested. The strongest source for the long-run claim is a 2014 review on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange that qualifies the claim. Among the key figures, the average short position of shares offered is 10.75 percent, covered in 22 transactions over 16.6 days in the aftermarket, and the loss of underwriting fees is 3.61 percent. Screening found no measured values for underpricing, long-run returns, retail investor demand, market sentiment or lock-up expiry.

text.triangulation: The corpus contains 32,707 papers, of which 14,089 support the claim that IPOs are underpriced on the first trading day, 6,126 qualify it, 1,262 contradict it and 11,230 are neutral. The contested percentage is 22.6, and the reading is described as mostly positive framing with a substantial cautionary minority. Only a small sample of documents was read: six were unrelated and three were unread, and the tier breakdown of the claim documents is three reviews, five articles and one preprint. Counter‑evidence tally shows one supporting document and nine unrelated, with no contradicting or qualifying documents, leading to the recommendation that the selected sample does not establish scientific consensus. This result does not reveal the methodological quality of the supporting papers nor the temporal distribution of the evidence. A careful researcher would seek additional, directly relevant sources and assess their design strength before drawing firm conclusions.
text.head_to_head: The comparison pits the underpricing claim against the long‑run underperformance claim. The underpricing claim has a corpus mix identical to the triangulation result and a contested percentage of 22.6, but no documents were read as supporting, contradicting or qualifying, only eight unrelated and one unread; its strongest source is unrelated. The underperformance claim shows 112 papers on both poles, a corpus mix of 28 supporting, 28 qualifying, 9 contradicting and 47 neutral, and a contested percentage of 33.0; one qualifying document was read and the strongest source qualifies the claim. The verdict states that the first claim has more evidence behind it. This analysis does not disclose the full set of papers examined nor the criteria for classifying sources as strongest. A careful researcher would retrieve and evaluate the underlying papers, especially those qualifying the underperformance claim, to verify the comparative assessment.
text.screening: The screening exercise returned null values for measured effect sizes for underpricing, long‑run returns, retail investor demand, market sentiment and lock‑up expiry, indicating no quantitative findings were located for these rows. Only the anchor investors row lists two papers, but provides no value, measure or population details. The source for the anchor investors row is "Response of anchor investors to pre‑IPO earnings management: evidence from an emerging market" (2023). This result does not indicate the direction or magnitude of any effect, nor does it confirm whether the lack of values reflects a true gap in the literature or a limitation of the search. A careful researcher would examine the two identified papers directly to extract any reported effect sizes and explore additional databases for the missing rows.
text.framing: Year‑by‑year percentages show that positive framing ranged from a high of 25.0 in 2024 to a low of 6.5 in 2023, while contested percentages varied between 7.4 in 2021 and 29.0 in 2023. The data suggest fluctuations in the tone of the literature over the period 2017‑2025, without a clear monotonic trend. The figures do not reveal the absolute number of papers contributing to each yearly percentage, nor the reasons behind the shifts. A careful researcher would investigate the underlying papers for each year to understand the drivers of the observed framing changes.
text.frontier: The frontier scan highlights six recent works, the most cited being "Initial Public Offerings Chinese Style" (2022) with 99 citations and a cautionary orientation. Other notable papers include a comparative study from 2023 (64 citations) and a critical piece on board independence (25 citations). The framing shift analysis reports a recent window of 80 papers with a cautionary proportion of 35.0, compared with an earlier window of 102 papers at 29.4, yielding a delta of 5.6 percentage points and a reading that framing is broadly unchanged. The caveat notes that orientation labels reflect the paper's own framing rather than an objective truth. This result does not quantify the impact of the new works on the broader field, nor does it identify which topics remain under‑explored. A careful researcher would read the highlighted papers to assess their contributions and monitor whether the modest increase in cautionary orientation influences future research directions.
text.gaps: The gap mapping breaks the underpricing claim into three components and finds evidence only for the systematic underpricing of IPOs, while the other two components – offering price set below market value and first trading day price exceeding offering price – have no evidence. This indicates that the literature addresses the overall phenomenon but not the specific mechanisms. The result does not assess the depth or quality of the evidence for the systematic underpricing component. A careful researcher would seek studies that explicitly test the missing components to determine whether the gaps are due to a true absence of research or to search limitations.

Contribution types are mainly empirical (179 papers) with fewer reviews (17), methodological (8) and theoretical (6) works. Topic distribution shows Corporate Finance and Governance as the largest area with 124 papers, and several other finance‑related topics ranging from 10 to 124 papers. The most cited works since 2020 all have zero citations, indicating they are very recent or have not yet attracted attention. This overview does not assess the quality or impact of the papers within each facet, nor does it show how the orientations relate to the claim under investigation. A careful researcher would prioritise reading the most cited and highly oriented papers to gauge the state of evidence.

Apply screening to identify which risk factors have measurable effect sizes, focusing on anchor investors where papers exist. Examine framing trends to understand how the tone of the literature has shifted over time, and consult the frontier scan for newly influential works and any subtle framing changes.
